44-92	S	shrub	17512	Kalmia buxifolia	Kalm. buxif.	Sandmyrtle	KALMIA	ERICACEAE	Heath Family	ERICALES	44-92	28 JAN 1992	1992	SD		W	collected directly from wild; origin known	Dilatush Nursery, 780 Route 130, Robbinsville, NJ 08691	Dilatush, T.			United States	New Jersey	Ocean Co.		7.5 minute series topo map, Jenkins Quadangle. Take Rte. 563 south from Chatsworth of Maxwell, turn right, take Iron Pipe Road to Hawkins Road, take Hawkins Road to its first fork, then angle left off Hawkins at the fork onto a much used unmarked sand road heading NW. Continue on this sand road to its first junction (marked "44" on the map). The joining roads are faint and old but an obvious "pull over" parking place on the right identifies the spot. After stopping it can be seen that an old trace road vaguely crosses here. A large number of Leiophyllum will be noted all around the immediate vicinity and for some distance near the tace road and beyond. Take the left trace road which shortly becomes a trail and continue southward on this trail over a sand hill and around a curve in the trail whereupon the trail meets a minor sand road. Continue (generally southward) on the sand road and you will encounter considerable Leiophyllum buxifolium and will pass several small "seasonal standing water ponds" (abandoned cranberry bogs) on the right.												The flower color of this Leiophyllum buxifolium population (overall in this area) varies from creamy white to pale pink. The creamy white ones have much lighter dormant season flower buds and like Kurume azaleas they also have a different (two year old leaves) autumn color that correlates with the flower and bud color.

PHYLLOSTACHYS	POACEAE	Grass Family	POALES	456-88	30 MAR 1988	1988	DV		W	collected directly from wild; origin known	Mr. Thomas Elias, U. S. National Arboretum, 3501 N. York Avenue, N.E., Washington, DC 20002 *via* 	United States Department of Agriculture, Washington, DC	McClure, F. A.			China	Lohkongtung			Beggar Mountain												[As Phyllostachys sp.] "Ka fat to chuk." This is a small bamboo, 2 to 3 meters high, and spreading by means of rhizomes. The young sprouts, which come in March and April, are considered by the local people to be very excellent, as it is not necessary to subject them to the parboiling and soaking process required by so many of the rhizome bamboos. Now and then a cane is said to appear with swollen nodes and shortened internodes, a characteristic no doubt responsible for the name given to this bamboo. Such canes are much sought after by the village people for pipestems.

United States	Alabama	Clark County		Near Grove Hill.											Populations were scattered but there were numerous plants within each. Collection of rooted plants was difficult due to most appearing to be interconnected within the colony. #'s 11 and 12 had distinctively different leaf shapes, and all plants within these groups appeared to be similar, lending further support to them being clonal. Plants range from 6" to 12-14'. Larger were reported but not seen. Seed capsules were found on some of the larger plants, scattered and not numerous. Capsules were batched when found except for #16, which Mr. Webb speculates might be a cross with H. virginiana. Mr. Webb speculates these tracts have been timbered 2 or 3 times before, but otherwise not disturbed. No evidence of fire. Most large plants were surrounded by low runners. #'s 10-13 are on private land scheduled to be clear cut in 2009. Mr. Webb will attempt to have at least the larger of these protected. #14 is on private land also scheduled to be clear cut and sprayed in 2009. A large mat form exists in this area but was not observed by us. Protection may not be possible. #'s 15-17 are on land owned by the Boy Scouts.	#2009-10 = 31°37.030'N, 087°48.608'W; #2009-11 = 31°37.051'N, 087°48.639'W; #2009-12 = 31°37.065'N, 087°48.143W; #2009-13 = no coordinates given; #2009-14 = no coordinated given; #2009-15 = 31°36.795'N, 087°48.949'W; #2009-17 = 31°36.773'N, 087°48.961'W.

Species of Maple	ACER	SAPINDACEAE	Soapberry Family	SAPINDALES	616-2010	22 OCT 2010	2010	SD		W	collected directly from wild; origin known	NACPEC 2010	Aiello, A. S., Dosmann, M., Wang, K.	NACPEC10		China	Shaanxi	Zha Shui	Ying Pan	Huang Hua Ling (Niu Bei Liang National Nature Reserve)	33	47	11	N	108	50	52	E	1697	M	Habit: tree: Height: 7m; D.B.H.: 15cm; Bark: gray; smooth; Leaves: opposite; 5 (7) lobes; serrate margins; abaxially pubescent @ vein axils; no milky sap; 7cm long x 7cm wide; Fruit: samaras; in terminal racemes on short spur branches; samaras nearly horizontal (180° angle)	This does not seem to fit any Acer listed in the Niu Bei Liang plant list. Reminiscent of Ginnala group but leaves do not fit. We saw about 6 different individuals. They were small trees. The stems had no diagnostic features - no colorful bark. The branches ended in a distinct, terminal, imbricated bud. The petioles and young twigs were green to red, and did have some lenticels. The leaves and petioles did not have milky sap. The leaves (about 5-6cm long and wide) usually had 5 lobes, but some had 7 lobes. The margins were serrated, and there was pubescence in the vein axils on the abaxial side. The infructescences seemed to all be terminal, with reddish brown samaras.

This site is the home of Art Lavigne, a practicing forester in his 80's, and supports 3 ~20-yr. old Castanea dentata. This stand supported ~15 trees and was right along Lake Champlain, which has a warming effect and often supports species that would not be expected this far north.

845-90			11389	Arctostaphylos x	Arcto. x		ARCTOSTAPHYLOS	ERICACEAE	Heath Family	ERICALES	845-90	12 OCT 1990	1990	SD	REF: 845-90 thru 860-90 -- The bulk of the collection is seed obtained from two fairly isolated populations of Arctostaphylos patula Greene x A. nevadensis v. coloradensis Rollins, and various backcrosses of these natural hybrids. Plants within these populations vary from nearly "typical A. nevadensis" to nearly "typical A. patula". Each packet of said seed is therefore marked as Arctostaphylos hybrid followed by a site designation (A or B) and the number of the plant it was collected from. These designations correspond to plants selected for clonal propagation and future selection by our nursery. I apologize that I cannot provide more correct nomenclature than Arctostaphylos hybrid; but these populations seem to be made up of almost nothing but promiscuous hybrids between the two parents, with only a few if any of the original sympatric species still existing. Additionally, many people consider A. nevadensis to be of hybrid origin itself (i.e., A. uva-ursi x A. patula). I should also note that no individuals in the populations were easily discernable as A. patula and no individuals of A. uva-ursi were found. Only plants of hybrid phenotype or of A. nevadensis phenotype were observed.	W	collected directly from wild; origin known	Dr. Zsolt Debreczy, Curator of World Herbarium, Botanical Dept. 5264	S	shrub	7478	Clethra alnifolia var. alnifolia 'Rosea'	Clethra aln. var. aln. 'Rosea'	Pink Summersweet	CLETHRA	CLETHRACEAE	Clethra Family	ERICALES	5264	27 JUN 1906	1906	CT		W	collected directly from wild; origin known	Dr. R.B. Handy, Fall River, MA	Handy, Louise Holmes			United States	Massachusetts	Fall River	Watuppa Lake												"Several years ago I found on the edge of Watuppa lake, Fall River, Massachusetts, one bush of Clethra alnifolia with pink petals. It was growing in company with a dozen or more bushes of the same species which had the ordinary white petals. Every year since it was first observed the pink-flowered individual has blossomed true to its color. Some seasons it has been badly killed back by the winter; but in all cases shoots from the root have exhibited the pink petals when they have flowered. Finding in the botanical works accessible to me no mention of a pink-flowered variety of this species I sent specimens to the Gray Herbarium where further literature was consulted but no reference to this variation of color was found. As most, if not all, works on our flora, which mention Clethra, state that its flowers are white, it seems worth while to put on record this attractive exception." -- L.H. Handy, Rhodora 9, 195-196.	Appears to have been the type locality for Clethra alnifolia f. rosea, as described by Rehder (MSD)
